script.t: Since the pandemic, millions of people have continued to work from home at least part of the week. With me is Dr Julia Grant, an organisational psychologist who has been studying the effects. Julia, is working from home good for us?

The honest answer is that it depends on the person and on how it's organised. Our research found that most people appreciate the flexibility. Not having to commute saves the average worker in our study about seventy minutes a day, and many use that time to exercise, sleep more or be with their families.
So what are the downsides?

The biggest one is that the boundary between work and home life disappears. When your office is your kitchen table, it's very tempting to check emails at ten o'clock at night. In our survey, home workers actually worked on average about an hour longer per day than office workers, and many reported that they found it hard to switch off.
And loneliness?

Yes, that's the second big issue, especially for younger employees who live alone or have just started their careers. They miss out on the informal learning that happens in an office, overhearing how experienced colleagues deal with a difficult client, for instance, or just asking a quick question at the next desk.
Is that why so many companies are now asking people to come back?

Partly. Some managers also simply feel more comfortable when they can see their staff, although there's very little evidence that productivity falls at home. In fact, for tasks that need deep concentration, like writing or analysis, people are often more productive at home, because there are fewer interruptions.
So what's your recommendation?

For most organisations, a hybrid model seems to work best, but the key is to be intentional about it. Office days should be used for things that really benefit from being together: brainstorming, training, building relationships. There's no point making people travel for an hour just to sit on video calls all day, which unfortunately happens a lot. And for individuals working at home, I'd say create a routine with a clear end to the day. Some people go for a short walk at six o'clock, as a kind of fake commute, to tell their brain that work is over.

script.t: Have you ever walked into a room and completely forgotten why you went there? Or met someone at a party and forgotten their name thirty seconds later? Most of us worry that these little lapses are a sign that something is wrong with our memory. But today I want to convince you that forgetting is not a failure. It's actually one of the brain's most useful features. More than a hundred years ago, a German psychologist called Hermann Ebbinghaus did a series of experiments on himself. He memorised lists of nonsense syllables, meaningless combinations like 'dax' or 'bup', and then tested himself at different intervals. What he found became known as the forgetting curve. Within twenty minutes, he had forgotten almost half of what he'd learned, and after a day, around seventy per cent. Ebbinghaus was surprised by how fast the loss happened, so he repeated the experiments many times over several years to make sure the results were reliable. Later researchers, using real words and real people instead of nonsense syllables, found very similar patterns. After that, the curve flattened out, and the little that remained stayed for a long time. Now, why would the brain throw away information so quickly? Imagine if you remembered every detail of every day: every number plate you saw, every conversation you overheard on the bus. You'd be overwhelmed. Forgetting acts like a filter, keeping what's important and getting rid of the rest. So how does the brain decide what's important? Mainly through repetition and meaning. Ebbinghaus discovered that if he reviewed the lists at increasing intervals, after one day, then three days, then a week, he forgot far less. This technique, now called spaced repetition, is used by many language learning apps. Meaning matters too. Information that connects to things we already know, or that makes us feel something, is much easier to remember than random facts. That's why you can remember the plot of a film you saw years ago but not the shopping list you wrote this morning. And that moment of walking into a room and forgetting why? Researchers think that passing through a doorway signals the brain that one scene has ended and another has begun, so it files away the previous one. So, if it happens to you, don't panic. Just go back through the door, and you'll probably remember.

title: Should cars be banned from city centres?

script.t: Tonight's question: should private cars be banned from our city centre? Oliver, you're on the city council and you support the plan.

I do. At the moment, our centre is dominated by traffic. Air pollution regularly exceeds safe levels, and the streets are noisy and dangerous for children and cyclists. Cities like Oslo and Pontevedra in Spain have removed most cars from their centres, and the results are impressive: cleaner air, fewer accidents, and more people walking and spending time in local shops.
Nadia, you run a small business in the centre. You're not convinced.

I'm not against the idea in principle. I want cleaner air too. But I'm worried about how it's being done. Many of my customers are older people who come from villages outside the city, where there are only two buses a day. If they can't drive in, they'll simply go to the big shopping centre on the motorway, which has free parking. Small shops like mine could close.

That's a fair concern, and it's why the plan includes three new park-and-ride sites, with buses into the centre every ten minutes. And disabled drivers, delivery vehicles and residents will still have access.

But park-and-ride only helps if it's cheap and reliable. The current bus service is neither. I've waited forty minutes for a bus in the rain more than once. I think the council should improve public transport first and then reduce car access gradually, not the other way round.
Let me bring in a question from our audience. Someone asks what will happen to the people who live in the centre and need their cars for work.
Residents will receive permits, so they can still drive to and from their homes. What we want to stop is people using the centre as a shortcut to cross the city.
Oliver, going back to Nadia's point, is it reasonable to improve public transport first?

I understand the argument, but if we wait for perfect public transport, we'll wait forever. Experience from other cities shows that when you reduce space for cars, people adapt faster than expected. Actually, in Pontevedra, many shops that had been afraid of the change ended up with more customers.

Maybe. But Pontevedra is a small city with a very compact centre. We're three times bigger. I'd like to see a trial first, perhaps closing a few streets for six months and measuring the effect on businesses.
Actually, that's something I'd be happy to propose to the council.

title: The story of the paperback
model: Cambridge B2 First – Listening Part 4 (radio feature)

script.t: In the summer of 1934, a publisher called Allen Lane was waiting at Exeter railway station after visiting the crime writer Agatha Christie. He looked around the station bookstall for something good to read on the long journey back to London, and found nothing but expensive hardback books and cheap magazines. That moment of frustration, the story goes, gave him an idea that would change reading forever. Lane wanted to publish high-quality books, serious novels and important non-fiction, at a price that ordinary working people could afford: sixpence, the same as a packet of cigarettes. Most people in the publishing industry thought he was mad. Paperbacks existed, but they were associated with cheap, poorly written stories, and booksellers worried that low prices would destroy their profits. Lane's own colleagues at the publishing company refused to support the project, so he and his two brothers financed it themselves. They chose a penguin as the logo, because it looked serious but friendly, and a young employee was sent to London Zoo to draw one. He came back with sketches of a penguin that he had spent the whole afternoon watching, and he complained afterwards that the animals smelled terrible. The drawing he made is still the basis of the logo today, although it has been redesigned several times. The first ten Penguin books appeared in 1935, including a novel by Ernest Hemingway. Bookshops ordered only small quantities. Then Lane had a breakthrough: he persuaded the chain store Woolworths, which sold everything from cooking pots to sweets, to place an order for sixty-three thousand copies. Suddenly, books were available to people who had never stepped into a bookshop. Within a year, Penguin had sold three million books. The design was also revolutionary. Instead of illustrations, the covers used simple horizontal bands of colour: orange for fiction, green for crime and blue for biographies. Readers could recognise the type of book instantly. Of course, not everyone was happy. The writer George Orwell, while admiring the books, worried that if books were so cheap, people would buy fewer new hardbacks and authors would earn less money. But history has proved Lane right. Cheap paperbacks helped create a mass reading public and, many argue, contributed to the growth of education in the twentieth century.

script.t: Tom Reeves works as a nutritionist for a professional football club. Tom, what does your job actually involve?

Basically, I make sure the players eat the right things at the right time to perform well and recover quickly. That means planning meals at the training ground, advising players on what to eat at home, and sometimes even teaching them to cook. You'd be surprised how many young players arrive at the club unable to make anything more complicated than toast.
Is it true that footballers eat huge amounts of pasta before a match?

Carbohydrates are important, yes, because they're the main fuel for high-intensity exercise. But the old idea of eating an enormous plate of pasta the night before is a bit outdated. Now we adjust the amount depending on the training load. On a light training day, players eat fewer carbohydrates and more vegetables and protein. Before a match, they increase the carbohydrates over a day or two, not just in one meal.
What about supplements? Many amateur athletes spend a lot of money on them.

In most cases, I'd say that money is wasted. A few supplements have good scientific evidence behind them, caffeine, for example, can genuinely improve performance. But most of the products you see in sports shops promise far more than they deliver. And there's a risk too: some supplements have been found to contain banned substances that aren't listed on the label, so professional players have to be extremely careful.
So how do you know if a supplement is worth taking?

Look for independent research, not the claims on the packet. And professional players should only use products that have been tested by an independent laboratory. If in doubt, speak to a qualified nutritionist before spending your money.
What's the most common mistake you see?

Not drinking enough. Even losing two per cent of your body weight through sweat can reduce performance noticeably. We weigh the players before and after training to see how much fluid they've lost, and then they have to replace it. The other big mistake is not eating soon enough after exercise. The first hour is when the muscles recover best.
And do the players ever eat junk food?
Of course! They're human. I don't believe in banning foods completely. If a player wants a burger after a match, that's fine. It's what they eat most of the time that matters.

script.t: When I told my friends I was going to travel around South America on my own for three months, most of them thought I was being reckless. I was thirty-four, I'd never travelled alone before, and my Spanish was limited to ordering coffee. To be honest, part of me agreed with them. The night before my flight to Lima, I barely slept. The first week was harder than I'd expected. It wasn't danger that was the problem; it was loneliness. I'd sit in restaurants on my own, pretending to read my phone, and feel that everybody was looking at me. Then, in a hostel in Cusco, I signed up for a four-day trek to Machu Picchu, and everything changed. There were nine of us in the group, from six different countries, and by the end of the trek we were like a family. Two of them, a Dutch couple, ended up travelling with me for the next three weeks. That was the first big lesson: when you're alone, you're much more open to meeting people, and they're more open to meeting you. The second lesson was about my own abilities. At home, I relied on my partner for everything practical, from booking trains to reading maps. In South America, I had no choice. When a bus broke down in the middle of the night in Bolivia, I had to negotiate a lift with a lorry driver in my terrible Spanish. He didn't speak any English, and I had to use gestures, drawings and a lot of smiling to explain where I needed to go. We drove for four hours through the mountains, sharing his sandwiches and listening to his favourite songs. It worked, and I felt incredibly proud. Of course, there were bad moments. I had my phone stolen in a market in La Paz, and I got quite ill after eating some street food. But even those experiences taught me that I could cope with problems without panicking. By the end of the trip, my Spanish had improved enormously, mostly thanks to the families I stayed with. Since coming home, I've been more confident at work, too. I'd recommend solo travel to anyone, at any age. Just start with somewhere that feels manageable, and be kind to yourself during the first difficult days.

script.t: Chloe, why do you have a sticker over your laptop camera? Are you worried someone's watching you?
Not really worried, just careful. It's actually quite common now. Even some very senior technology executives do it.
I think people are getting a bit paranoid about privacy. I've got nothing to hide, so I don't really care what companies know about me.

I used to think that too. But it's not just about hiding things. Last year I downloaded all the data that one social media app had collected about me. It was a huge file. They knew every place I'd been, every advert I'd clicked on, even messages I'd typed and then deleted without sending.
Seriously? Messages you never sent?

Some apps record what you type before you send it. And the point is, they use all this information to predict what you'll buy, what you'll believe, even your mood. Then they sell access to you to advertisers.
But surely they need my permission to do that?

Technically, you give it when you accept the terms and conditions. Has anyone ever actually read those? They can be longer than a novel. Most people just click accept without thinking, and that's what companies are counting on.
I definitely never read them. OK, that's a bit creepy. But the services are free. That's the deal, isn't it?
That's exactly the problem. If you're not paying for the product, then you are the product. I'm not saying we should all stop using these apps. I still use them. But I've changed a few things.
Like what?

I turned off location tracking for most apps, because why does a torch app need to know where I am? I use a different browser that blocks trackers. And I've stopped doing those online quizzes, the ones like 'Which film character are you?' They're often just a way to collect personal information.
Oh no, I did one of those yesterday. It asked for my mother's maiden name and the name of my first pet.
Ben! Those are typical security questions for bank accounts! You should change them as soon as possible.
Right. Maybe I'm not as careful as I thought.

script.t: Good morning. Today I'd like to talk about a learning strategy that is surprisingly effective, and surprisingly under-used: learning by teaching. You've probably noticed that when you explain something to a friend, you suddenly understand it better yourself. Psychologists call this the protégé effect, and there's a lot of research to support it. In one well-known study, students were divided into two groups and given the same text to study. One group was told they would be tested on it. The text was about a scientific topic that none of them had studied before, and they had the same amount of time to prepare. The other group was told they would have to teach it to other students. In fact, neither group taught anyone. Both groups took the same test. But the students who expected to teach scored significantly higher. Simply preparing to teach changed the way they studied. They organised the information more carefully, looked for the key points and tried to anticipate questions. Actually teaching has even stronger effects. When you have to explain an idea out loud, gaps in your understanding become obvious very quickly. You might think you understand how a car engine works, until a curious child asks you why. Researchers have also found that teaching increases motivation. In one experiment with children, those who had to teach a virtual student on a computer, a cartoon character that 'learned' from them, put more effort into learning than those who studied for themselves. They seemed to feel responsible for their student's progress. Some of them even said they felt embarrassed when their character made mistakes, as if it reflected badly on them. So how can you use this? You don't need a real class. You can explain a topic to a friend or family member who knows nothing about it, or even to an empty room. Some students record themselves giving a short lesson and then listen back. Another technique, named after the physicist Richard Feynman, is to write an explanation of a concept as if you were teaching it to a twelve-year-old, using simple words. Wherever you get stuck or start using complicated vocabulary to hide confusion, that's the part you need to study again. Next week, you'll all have a chance to try this, because each of you will teach the group for ten minutes.

script.t: Amira Haddad started a mobile coffee business from an old van five years ago. Today she has four cafés. Amira, how did it all begin?

I was working in marketing for a big company, and I was completely bored. I'd always loved coffee, and during a holiday in Australia I saw how good the coffee culture was there, even in small towns. When I came back, I bought an old delivery van, spent six months turning it into a mobile café, and started parking it outside the train station every morning.
Was it successful immediately?

Not at all. The first winter was awful. It was cold, it rained constantly, and some days I sold fewer than twenty coffees. I seriously thought about giving up. What saved me was the regular customers. A few commuters started coming every day, and they told their colleagues. By the spring, there was a queue every morning.
What was the biggest mistake you made?

Trying to do everything myself for too long. I was making the coffee, doing the accounts, posting on social media and repairing the van. I was working sixteen-hour days and I got ill. Eventually I realised I needed to hire someone, and it was the best decision I ever made. My first employee, Jake, is now the manager of our biggest café.
How did you choose the location?

I spent two weeks counting people at different times of day in different places. The train station was the busiest in the mornings, and there was no other coffee shop nearby, only a vending machine with terrible coffee. That made the decision easy.
What makes your cafés different?

We buy our beans directly from small farms in Ethiopia and Colombia, so we know exactly where they come from and the farmers get a fair price. And we try to create a community feeling. We know most customers' names, and we host events like poetry evenings and board game nights.
Any advice for people thinking about starting a business?

Start small and test your idea before you invest everything. The van was perfect for that, because if it had failed, I could have sold it. And be prepared for the difficult times. Every business has them. The important thing is not to make decisions when you're exhausted.

title: The return of the white stork

script.t: For more than six hundred years, white storks were absent from the skies of Britain. These large birds, with their long red legs and black and white wings, were once common across Europe, building enormous nests on church towers and chimneys. In Britain, the last recorded breeding pair nested on the roof of St Giles' Cathedral in Edinburgh in 1416. After that, they disappeared, probably because they were hunted for food and their wetland habitats were drained for farming. In 2016, a group of conservation organisations decided to try to bring them back. The project is based at Knepp, a large estate in the south of England where farmland has been allowed to return to a wilder state. The team brought young storks from Poland, where the species is still common, and kept them in a large protected area for a time, so that they would get used to the place and consider it home. During that time, they were fed and checked regularly by vets, and the team watched carefully to see whether they were behaving naturally. When the gates were finally opened, the young birds began to explore the surrounding countryside, but most of them returned to the estate every evening. Storks are migratory birds. Each autumn, most European storks fly south to spend the winter in Africa, travelling thousands of kilometres. The big question was whether the British storks would return after their first migration. To find out, scientists attached small, lightweight tracking devices to some of the birds. The data showed fascinating journeys. One stork flew through France and Spain to Morocco, and then came back to Sussex the following spring, covering more than four thousand kilometres. In 2020, a pair of storks built a nest in an oak tree at Knepp and successfully raised three chicks, the first wild-born storks in Britain for centuries. Since then, more pairs have bred each year. Local people have welcomed the birds enthusiastically, and the storks have become something of a tourist attraction, with guided walks to see the nests. However, the project's leaders warn that the population is still small and fragile. Storks need wet grasslands full of insects, frogs and small fish, and these habitats remain rare in Britain. The future of the storks, they say, depends on restoring much more of the landscape they once relied on.
